I get tired of replacing burned out bulbs and, since presumably LEDs would last longer, I'm thinking about switching. But the ones I've tested seemed very dim. Has anyone done this with good results?
Replacing incandescent bulbs with LEDs: a good idea or not?

Yes, LEDs ideally will last longer. I'd had a few fail on me, but that number is very low considering the hundreds I've installed.

I've replaced almost all my incandescent with LED. I usually colour match the LED for the insert and it improves the colour on the playfield. It depends on the colour, but reds, blues, greens are a major improvement. Some yellows and oranges are. It just depends on the insert. My playfields really pop now.

For GI, it depends. Sometimes incandescent look better depending on the theme.

LED strips can be fitted into places incandescent can't fit giving your table better lighting. I've put red LED strips under red plastic ramps and the whole thing glows. With incandescent, it just looked like a couple spots of light under a ramp.

The major benefit is power draw. Machines use less power and run cooler.

My only minor complaint against LED is how they blink. When an incandescent blinks, it ramps up brightness and fades out. LEDs go on and off. For machines that flash every bulb at once, this can be visually jarring with LEDs. Also, if you have something like 10 bulbs in a row and the machine chases the light across the 10 bulbs quickly, sometimes it can look a little funky with LED - not as smooth as with incandescent.

Overall, I prefer the LED though. They can visually breathe new life into an older machine.

Check out the LEDs from Comet Pinball. I used those on my last machine and they were good.

Thanks for that very useful information. What do you think about the idea of buying a few LEDs from Comet Pinball as a test? What about the dimness I've observed with the LEDs I tried previously? Do you think maybe I just got the wrong ones? They definitely weren't specifically designed for pinball machines.

If they weren't designed for pinball, that's probably the reason they were dim. Were the ones you used made for cars?

LEDs for pinball have the specific voltages in mind. All the ones I've used have been bright and vibrant.

Defiantly, buy a sample from Comet and test them out.

Out of curiosity, what pinball machine are you putting these in?
That sounds encouraging. I'll order some from Comet. They'll go in the 1970s vintage Bally Star Trek and Bally Xenon. Both are fully functional at this time.

For most feature and GI lights, the regular 44/46 and 555 bulbs shouldn't have any problems. Some pinball circuits provide a little power down the lines which is enough to trigger a small amount of light on LEDs. They call this ghosting. I have this on a few spots on my machines but it doesn't bother me because the light is very faint. It really bothers some people though. They make non-ghosting LEDs which I believe has a small circuit that acts as a suppressor. It won't light the LED until the voltage goes over a particular amount. I only buy non-ghosting LEDs now. They're only a few cents more. I would recommend those.

For flashers, you might need to make a small modification. Flasher bulbs, like the 89 size, sometimes have what they call a warming circuit. It basically provides a current to the bulb and keeps the filament warm. Then when the bulb gets the voltage to flash, it gets brighter because the filament isn't starting from a cold point. This is fine for incandescent, but with LED the warming circuit voltage is enough to light the LED. You'll know if you have one of those circuits because when you put the LED in it will stay lighted.

You can remove the warming circuit by simply disconnecting it. I only had to do this on one machine so far. I just clipped the lines and put a piece of tape on them which says what it is. Then in the future if someone has the machine and wants to restore it back to incandescent, it's easy for them.
Absolutely. Less heat, less power, less wear. They make warm white ones if you still want the incandescent look, though I only prefer this for very old machines. LEDs 4 life.

I've on my third non-profit, and the second I've started (shared workshop). It's fun, in a masochistic kind of way. We've wound up using spreadsheets to track finances for the first few years, until we can justify quickbooks or something. Your needs will be different than mine, however, because you're an entirely different type of organization in a different country.

I'd recommend finding an accountant or bookkeeper or similar to volunteer hours to help. You may run into a situation where a funder wants to audit your books, and it will really help having a dedicated staff member who can handle the request and provide a nice report to help sell the organization.

For marketing, you'll have a target audience, and will have to tailor your message to them. Posters stapled to lamp posts isn't going to get the yacht club set to open their wallets, but they might not be your target either - figure out who is. On that site which will not be named, there's an entrepreneur discussion group that occasionally has marketing advice come up, or offers of assistance on figuring out marketing - it would be a good resource.

Don't worry about the lack of business skills - you're not running a business. Worry about the lack of communication skills, and consider bringing experts on to the team to help you.

In our area, a non profit has a board of directors to run things, making it hard to structure with one person. We use this to our advantage to bring on the key initial stakeholders to make sure all of our bases are covered. We try to bring in people with technical skills (usually one or two), a person with financial skills and/or contacts who can act as treasurer, and a person with political contacts (makes zoning stuff, etc, much easier). Once we're operational, we bring in volunteers or compensated individuals (membership, access, financial) to cover gaps like marketing, social media, and organizational skills.

There has been talk lately about incarceration rates, including that of non-violent drug offenders.

In an economic sense, what would happen if we released all of these drug dealers back into the streets? Would there be less new drug dealers because of some sort of "job scarcity"?

If so, does that mean incarcerating low drug dealers encourage mean that we are opening spots for others to take their place? Or in other words, does the fact that we arrest so many drug dealers mean we create more drug dealers?
What would happen to the drug trade we reduced/released non-violent drug offenders?

In an economic sense, what would happen if we released all of these drug dealers back into the streets? Would there be less new drug dealers because of some sort of "job scarcity"?<

If it was just a mass release, you would see a massive increase in crime. Most of the people in jail do not have an education nor do they possess any desirable skills. In the job market today, that means you won't get hired. If you are starving, have no home, and have no money; robbing a place begins to sound like a viable option. How you get around this would require some pretty serious changes to prisoner release and behaviour.

If so, does that mean incarcerating low drug dealers encourage mean that we are opening spots for others to take their place? Or in other words, does the fact that we arrest so many drug dealers mean we create more drug dealers?<

If we were legalize marijuana the laws of supply and demand start to take over. Since you have more product, you will see prices go down. With the dealer's profits lower, selling other items drugs start to happen. The demand for heroin is much lower then pot. Most people know that smoking a joint will not kill you, but everyone knows heroin is something you just don't mess around with if you can help it. You would have a glut at the beginning because everyone would go smoke a joint legally. Once the novelty wears off, you will go back to the same number of people who used before, but now wouldn't have to worry about getting busted by the cops.

If we truly wanted to cut crime legalizing pot would be the quickest and easiest way to do so.

To answer your second question- yes, every time one drug dealer gets arrested, three more pop up to try to take over the business. The demand for illegal drugs has never gone down, and someone will always move in to supply the demand.

Low income areas are rife with desperate individuals looking for a way to elevate themselves. Desperate people are more inclined to take risks to make money. The illegal drug market holds a nearly irresistible allure- there are no real skills required and there will always be customers.

Others have commented that there would be a massive rise in crime if all the nonviolent drug offenders were released from prison. This might be true. But I believe it is a far greater crime keeping them locked up in the first place. I also feel that it's time for society to own up to the awful mistake we made in allowing drugs to be criminalized in the first place. Let them go free and let's get some rehabilitation programs in place to help put these people to work.
